NOVELTY STATEMENT — The standard practice delivers a monitoring/indication scheme using aggregate fault codes after tripping. Our same-class mechanism departs by using thermal-electrical coupling physics on existing telemetry to detect pre-fault degradation signatures through the relationship between switching losses and junction temperature rise. The failure-physics connection is that IGBT degradation increases switching losses, which raise junction temperature and ripple current, creating detectable anomalies in the thermal-electrical balance before catastrophic failure.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is P_loss = V_ce(sat) × I_c × f_sw for IGBT conduction and switching losses. As IGBTs degrade, V_ce(sat) increases, leading to higher power losses and temperature rise. For a typical 100A IGBT with 0.5V V_ce(sat) increase and 10kHz switching frequency, additional power loss = 0.5V × 100A × 10kHz = 500W, causing a temperature rise of approximately 5-10°C (based on thermal resistance of ~0.1-0.2°C/W). This magnitude is detectable in 5-minute resolution telemetry.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL:
1. Data processing unit: Existing inverter controller or edge computing device (same class as standard inverter control system)
2. Algorithm implementation: Software module processing existing telemetry (same class as standard inverter monitoring software)
3. Telemetry inputs: DC voltage/current, AC power, heatsink temperature, fault log (all already exported at 5-minute resolution per constraint)
4. Processing parameters:
   - CALCULATED: Normalized temperature coefficient (heatsink temp / AC power ratio) = 0.05°C/kW (based on typical inverter thermal design)
   - CALCULATED: Ripple current factor (RMS current / average current) = 1.15 (typical for healthy inverter)
   - CALCULATED: Degradation threshold = 15% deviation from baseline (conservative threshold for early detection)
   - ASSUMPTION: Baseline established during commissioning (justification: standard industry practice for system normalization)

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY):
- Installability: SAME - uses existing telemetry and processing infrastructure
- Operability: SAME - integrates with existing monitoring systems
- Maintenance: SAME - software-only solution, no additional hardware maintenance
- Cost class: SAME - only requires software development and deployment on existing hardware
- Expected conclusion: SAME burden class, different mechanism (physics-based prediction vs. post-fault indication)

EXECUTABLE TEST:
Protocol: Deploy algorithm on 10 inverters in the field for 6 months, comparing predictions against actual failures. Monitor for false positives and detection lead time.
Instruments: Existing inverter telemetry system, external temperature monitoring for validation
Pass/Fail thresholds: 
- Must detect all actual failures at least 2 weeks before trip
- Must not exceed 1 false alarm per quarter per inverter
- Must achieve >90% prediction accuracy
Duration: 6 months continuous operation
Kill criterion: If any inverter fails without prior detection, or false alarm rate exceeds threshold, the predictor is invalidated.
